concepts.title: Looking at Individual Pixels
concepts.one_liner: The image in @fig-pexels-retha-ferguson is a tiny image with just $32 \times 32$ pixels.
concepts.content:
Before we build systems that can see, it is good to learn to look at images and to pay attention to individual pixels. The image in @fig-pexels-retha-ferguson is a tiny image with just $32 \times 32$ pixels.

What is the minimum number of pixels needed to form a recognizable image? The answer depends on the image. It is possible to create visually recognizable images with very few pixels @torralba_2009.

It is so small that we can actually look at each single pixel and think about how it is that we can make sense of it. For instance, let's look at the pixel in row 13 counting from the bottom, and column 12 counting from the left. That pixel corresponds to a dark gray pixel, which is near a couple of other pixels with similar intensity, surrounded by a set of white pixels. That pixel seems to be a pen, but how do we know what it is? The pen is barely three pixels long and one pixel wide. How can that provide enough information?

![A tiny image with 32 $\times$ 32 color pixels. Despite the very low resolution, we can still recognize most of its content. *Source*: Original image created with Dall-E, and downsampled with Photoshop.](figures/visionscience/DALLE_32x32.png){#fig-pexels-retha-ferguson width="90%"}

Same image as in @fig-pexels-retha-ferguson but shown small and blurred to remove the artifacts due to the square pixels.

[FIGURE:5ebf18ba45aa5415 | A very low-resolution, 32 by 32 pixel image of a person sitting at a desk. Despite the extreme blurriness, one can discern a person's head and shoulder on the right, a blue mug in the center, a pen...]

Reducing the size and blurring helps better recognizing the objects despite containing the same visual information.

Recognition of the meaning of that pixel can not come just from the intensity of that pixel or the few pixels nearby. There are way too many possible situations in which different objects in the world could map to a similar set of pixel intensities. Instead, is the whole image and the context of the pen that provides the necessary information to recognize the pen. Taken in isolation, those pixels are impossible to recognize. Here we show, from left to right, the hand, the blue mug, and the pen.

concepts.motivation_md: Understanding individual pixels helps us grasp how minimal visual information can still form recognizable images, which is crucial for building systems that interpret images effectively.
concepts.recap_md:
- Images can be recognizable even with very few pixels, such as $32 \times 32$.
- Recognition depends on the context of the whole image, not just individual pixel intensities.
- Blurring low-resolution images can help in recognizing objects despite pixelation.

concepts.title: Vision is a dynamical system

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: Vision is a dynamical system, even when looking at a static image.
concepts.content: Visual perception cannot be formulated as a simple input-output function over predefined domains. Vision is a dynamical system, even when looking at a static image. The longer you look at an image, the more details you see and the better you understand the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Vision is not a static process; it evolves over time as you observe an image, revealing more details and improving understanding, which simple input-output models cannot capture.
concepts.recap_md:
- Visual perception is not a simple input-output function.
- Vision operates as a dynamical system.
- Longer observation of an image reveals more details and understanding.

concepts.title: a big image like this contains thousands of tiny images within it

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: A big image like this contains thousands of tiny images within it.
concepts.content: As you look around the image, notice that each patch you look at is actually a small photo in its own right. In fact, a big image like this contains thousands of tiny images within it (@fig-tiny_images). A single photo can be *big data*; if you chop up this photo you get a big dataset of tiny images. A common trick in computer vision is to take a method that was developed for processing a dataset and instead apply it to the set of patches in an image, or vice versa.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept shows how a single large image can be viewed as a dataset of many small images, enabling techniques from dataset processing to be applied to image patches, which is useful in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- A large image contains thousands of tiny images within it.
- A single photo can be considered big data.
- Methods for datasets can be applied to image patches and vice versa.

concepts.title: The tiny holes between the leaves of a tree create a multitude of pinholes
aliases: pinhole camera effect in tree shadows
concepts.one_liner: The tiny holes between the leaves of a tree create a multitude of pinholes that project images of the sun on the ground.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept explains why the bright spots under a tree's shadow appear circular and similar in size, revealing that the tiny holes between leaves act as pinhole cameras projecting images of the sun.
concepts.recap_md:
- Tiny holes between leaves act as pinhole cameras projecting images of the sun.
- Bright spots on the ground under a tree are circular and similar in size, not irregular.
- The shape of the projected light spots is dominated by the shape of the sun when openings are small.

key_passage.text: One of the most common situations that we often encounter is the pinhole cameras formed by the spacing between the leaves of a tree. The tiny holes between the leaves of a tree create a multitude of pinholes. The pinholes created by the leaves project different copies of the sun on the floor. When the openings between leaves are small enough, the shape of the projected spot light is dominated by the shape of the sun.

motivation.text: But something is a bit odd about the shape of the bright spots projected on the floor. We would expect that the spots of light would have irregular shapes as the openings between leaves will have all kinds of irregular profiles. Instead, as shown in the figure, the spots appear to be circular and of similar size. This observation already puzzled Aristotle.

example.text: When walking under the shadow of a tree on a bright sunny day when the sun is right above us, we can see how some light rays get through the holes left between leaves, creating spots on the floor.

concepts.title: orientation perception from vanishing points
concepts.one_liner: The orientation of a surface in an image can be perceived from the positions of vanishing points where parallel lines intersect.
concepts.content:
Looking at the previous picture of the shadow of the tree, another interesting question comes to mind: How do you know you are looking at a picture of the ground? How do you know the orientation of the camera?

Look at the two drawings in @fig-vertical_or_horizontal. The lines in the drawing on the left correspond to tiles in a floor, the line drawing on the right is the same drawing rotated 90 degrees. Which one seems to be a horizontal surface and which one seems vertical? Why? The differences in the line orientations are subtle and yet produce a very different perception.

![Line drawings. The one on the left seems to correspond to an horizontal surface while the one on the right looks like a vertical surface.](figures/visionscience/vertical_or_horizontal.png){#fig-vertical_or_horizontal width="100%"}

In the arrangement on the left, there are two vanishing points (the points where parallel lines intersect) and both are above the drawing, compatible with the horizon line. However, in the drawing on the right, one of the vanishing points is below the figure and gives the impression that the camera is looking at a vertical wall (the camera seems to be higher than the visible part of the wall). The horizon line of the plane (the line that connects both vanishing points) is horizontal in the left drawing and vertical in the right one.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding orientation perception from vanishing points helps explain how subtle differences in line orientations in images lead to different perceptions of surface orientation and camera viewpoint.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vanishing points are where parallel lines appear to intersect in an image.
- The position of vanishing points relative to the image indicates surface orientation.
- Horizontal horizon lines correspond to horizontal surfaces; vertical horizon lines correspond to vertical surfaces.

key_passage.text: In the arrangement in the left, there are two **vanishing points** (the points in which parallel lines intersect) and both are above the drawing, compatible with the horizon line. However, on the drawing on the right, one of the vanishing points is below the figure and gives the impression that the camera is looking at a vertical wall (the camera seems to be higher than the visible part of the wall). The horizon line of the plane (the line that connects both vanishing points) is horizontal in the left drawing and vertical on the right one.

concepts.title: motion blur
concepts.one_liner: Blur in photos taken from a moving car occurs because the camera sensor collects light over time while the car moves, averaging multiple shifted images.
concepts.content:
When we are in a moving car and take a picture from the passenger window, images often appear blurred, especially at night (@fig-Paris_from_moving_car). This blur occurs because the camera sensor collects light during a period while the car is moving, resulting in a picture that is the average of several translated copies of the same image. However, not all objects are equally blurry; distant objects may still look sharp while nearby objects appear very blurry.

The amount of blur depends on the car's speed, the camera's exposure time, and the distance between the camera and each object in the scene. Further discussion on how camera motion relates to distance will follow.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion blur explains why photos taken from moving vehicles often appear smeared, helping us understand how camera movement, exposure time, and object distance affect image sharpness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Motion blur happens when a camera captures light over time while moving, averaging shifted images.
- Nearby objects appear blurrier than distant ones due to relative motion.
- The amount of blur depends on speed, exposure time, and object distance.

key_passage.text: Blur is due to the fact that the camera sensor is collecting light during a period of time while the car is moving and the picture that results is the average of several translated copies of the same image.

motivation.text: The amount of blur is related to the car speed, the exposure time, and the distance between the camera and each object in the scene.

concepts.title: principle of continuity
concepts.one_liner: The gestalt psychologists called this the principle of continuity, where smooth, continuous line segments are assumed to lie on a single object because it's quite a coincidence for two objects to line up perfectly.
concepts.content:
Principle of continuity. In the following drawing, we see one wave and one line:

[FIGURE:2962e76f5808a7be | A schematic drawing of a horizontal straight line intersected by a continuous sinusoidal wave. The wave oscillates symmetrically above and below the line, completing approximately two and a half...]

Despite this, other groupings are also possible.

[FIGURE:d7efe27713f24942 | A sequence of five parabolic shapes alternating between facing up and facing down, arranged along a horizontal axis. The shapes are disconnected, with three upward-facing arches on top and two...]

We learned about the generic view principle in , and this idea comes up a lot in computer vision. But it turns out that in most photographs it's easy to find accidents. This is because photos contain so many things, thousands of tiny images, and there are so many coincidences that could occur. @fig-visionscience-migrant_mother shows a famous photo and we will look for some coincidences in it. The coincidences are of a specific variety: generically, if you see smooth, continuous line segments you assume that they lie on a single object because it's quite a coincidence for two objects to line up just so their contours perfectly align. The gestalt psychologists called this the **principle of continuity**. The insets for @fig-visionscience-migrant_mother show several locations in the photo "Migrant Mother" by Dorothea Lange where exactly this happens. Can you find more?

![Source: Migrant Mother (1936), by Dorothea Lange. On the right are four examples of coincidences that violate the Gestalt principle of continuity. From top-left clockwise: finger boundary aligns with lip contour, cloth aligns with eye, creases align on two different shirts, sleeve boundary is tangent to line on a different shirt.](figures/visionscience/accidents_migrant_mother.jpg){#fig-visionscience-migrant_mother width="100%"}
concepts.motivation_md: The principle of continuity helps us interpret visual scenes by assuming that smooth, continuous lines belong to the same object, reducing ambiguity caused by coincidental alignments in images.
concepts.recap_md:
- The principle of continuity assumes smooth, continuous line segments belong to a single object.
- It explains why perfectly aligned contours in images are unlikely to be coincidental.
- Gestalt psychologists identified this principle to understand visual perception and object grouping.

concepts.title: accidental coincidences
concepts.one_liner: In most photographs, it's easy to find accidental coincidences where contours of different objects align perfectly, violating the Gestalt principle of continuity.
concepts.content:
We learned about the generic view principle, and this idea comes up a lot in computer vision. However, in most photographs, it's easy to find accidents because photos contain so many things—thousands of tiny images—and there are so many coincidences that could occur. @fig-visionscience-migrant_mother shows a famous photo, and we will look for some coincidences in it. The coincidences are of a specific variety: generically, if you see smooth, continuous line segments, you assume they lie on a single object because it's quite a coincidence for two objects to line up so that their contours perfectly align. The gestalt psychologists called this the principle of continuity. The insets for @fig-visionscience-migrant_mother show several locations in the photo "Migrant Mother" by Dorothea Lange where exactly this happens. Can you find more?

![Source: Migrant Mother (1936), by Dorothea Lange. On the right are four examples of coincidences that violate the Gestalt principle of continuity. From top-left clockwise: finger boundary aligns with lip contour, cloth aligns with eye, creases align on two different shirts, sleeve boundary is tangent to line on a different shirt.](figures/visionscience/accidents_migrant_mother.jpg){#fig-visionscience-migrant_mother width="100%"}
concepts.motivation_md: Photographs contain many elements, making accidental alignments of contours common; understanding these coincidences helps explain visual perception and challenges assumptions about object boundaries.
concepts.recap_md:
- Photographs often contain accidental coincidences where contours of different objects align.
- The Gestalt principle of continuity assumes smooth contours belong to a single object.
- Violations of this principle can be seen in famous photos like "Migrant Mother" by Dorothea Lange.

concepts.title: raindrops as natural light field
concepts.one_liner: Every raindrop refracts a panorama of the scene around it, showing hundreds of images from slightly different angles, similar to what light field cameras capture.
concepts.content: When it rains you get to see a rare sight. Every raindrop refracts a panorama of the scene around it (@fig-droplets). What you are seeing is not just one photo but hundreds of images of the scene, one in each raindrop, all from slightly different angles. It turns out specially designed cameras have been made that do the same thing, and they are called **light field cameras**. These cameras use an array of tiny lenses rather than raindrops, but the result is similar: they capture what the scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles, and from that density of information they can achieve many interesting tricks, such as triangulating the depth of objects in the scene and synthetically refocusing the image after it has been taken.
concepts.motivation_md: Raindrops naturally capture multiple views of a scene from different angles, inspiring the design of light field cameras that record rich visual information for depth and refocusing effects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Every raindrop refracts a panorama of the scene around it, showing multiple images from different angles.
- Light field cameras mimic this by using arrays of tiny lenses to capture many viewing angles.
- This dense information enables depth triangulation and synthetic refocusing after capture.

concepts.title: image as lossy projection
concepts.one_liner: An image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state, collapsing 3D geometry into a flat 2D grid and occluding much of the scene.
concepts.content:
In the *Allegory of the Cave*, Plato imagined a group of prisoners chained up in a cave whose only experience of the outside world is through shadows cast on the cave's wall. When we look at images, we think we are directly seeing reality, but actually the situation is much more like Plato's cave. An image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state. It collapses all the 3D geometry into a flat 2D grid of pixels. From any given viewing angle, most of the scene is occluded. Materials are only depicted in terms of how photons bounce off their surfaces; what's below the surface may be completely omitted. When you look at a picture, think about all the things you cannot see. There's more you don't see than you do. One job of a vision system is to infer everything you can't see given everything you can.

The allegory of the cave has several layers of indirection: the shadows are cast by puppets that are controlled by puppeteers who act out interpretations of the broader reality outside.
concepts.motivation_md: Images only show a limited, flattened view of reality, hiding much of the 3D structure and unseen details; understanding this helps vision systems infer the full scene from incomplete data.
concepts.recap_md:
- An image collapses 3D geometry into a 2D grid of pixels.
- Most of the scene is occluded or omitted in an image.
- Vision systems must infer unseen aspects from visible information.

concepts.title: material perception wetness

position.section_title: How Do You Know Something Is Wet?

concepts.one_liner: We can recognize if something is wet or not without touching it, as shown in @fig-wet_sand.
concepts.content:
Our visual system allows us to recognize not just objects, but also material. We can tell if something will feel hot or cold, soft or hard, smooth or rugged. We can also recognize if something is wet or not without touching it, as shown in @fig-wet_sand.

Why does sand look darker when it's wet? Does everything wet look darker than when it is dry? How can we tell which parts of the sand are dark because they are wet and which ones are dark because they are under a shadow?
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing wetness visually helps us understand material properties without physical contact, which is essential for interpreting our environment and making decisions based on appearance alone.
concepts.recap_md:

- Wet sand appears darker, raising questions about visual cues distinguishing wetness from shadows.
- Understanding visual wetness perception aids in material recognition.
